{"title":"å, ä and ö are letters of their own","body":"Swedish has 29 letters: the 26 of English, then å, ä and ö, in that order at the end of the alphabet. They are not a or o with marks, and a dictionary files them after z.","sources":[{"title":"Swedish alphabet (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_alphabet"}]}

{"title":"Long and short","body":"A stressed syllable is long: either its vowel is long, or the vowel is short and the consonant after it is long. A double consonant in spelling marks the short vowel: tak /tɑːk/, tack /takː/. Length changes the vowel too: long a is /ɑː/ and short a is /a/, long u is /ʉː/ and short u is /ɵ/. The chart shows the nine long vowels.","sources":[{"title":"Engstrand (1990), Swedish, Journal of the IPA","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/S0025100300004060"},{"title":"Help:IPA/Swedish (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish"}]}

{"title":"The sj-sound /ɧ/","body":"A voiceless sound made with the back of the tongue, lips slightly rounded. It is spelled sj, skj, stj, sk before e, i, y, ä or ö, and -ti- in words such as station.","sources":[{"title":"Help:IPA/Swedish (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish"}]}

{"title":"The tj-sound /ɕ/","body":"A soft voiceless hiss with the middle of the tongue raised, with no t in it. It is spelled tj, kj, and k before e, i, y, ä or ö: kjol, tjugo, köpa.","sources":[{"title":"Help:IPA/Swedish (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish"}]}

{"title":"Two word accents","body":"A word stressed on a syllable that another follows has one of two pitch patterns. Accent 1 is marked here with ̌ on the stressed vowel and accent 2 with ̂: anden /ˈǎndɛn/ \"the duck\", anden /ˈândɛn/ \"the spirit\". Most words of two syllables, and almost every compound, take accent 2; the day names, such as måndag, take accent 1. A word of one syllable has no contrast and no mark.","sources":[{"title":"Engstrand (1990), Swedish, Journal of the IPA","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/S0025100300004060"},{"title":"Help:IPA/Swedish (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish"}]}

{"title":"Numbers as they are said","body":"The transcriptions give the careful forms. In everyday speech nio and tio are /ˈnîːɛ/ and /ˈtîːɛ/, and the tens drop their last vowel: trettio is /ˈtrɛ̂tːɪ/, fyrtio /ˈfœ̂ʈːɪ/. Hundra and tusen also come as etthundra and ettusen.","sources":[{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"},{"title":"Wiktionary på svenska","url":"https://sv.wiktionary.org/"}]}

{"title":"r with t, d, n, s or l","body":"In Central Standard Swedish r merges with a following t, d, n, s or l into one sound made with the tip of the tongue raised just behind the gum ridge: ʈ, ɖ, ɳ, ʂ, ɭ. So fjorton is /ˈfjûːʈɔn/ and arton /ˈɑ̂ːʈɔn/, with no separate r.","sources":[{"title":"Help:IPA/Swedish (English Wikipedia)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish"}]}

{"title":"gn is /ŋn/","body":"After a vowel, gn is said /ŋn/, with the ng of English \"sing\": regn /rɛŋn/, lugn.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"The ending -igt","body":"The g of -igt is silent: soligt /ˈsûːlɪt/, molnigt, blåsigt. The ending makes the form of an adjective that goes with ett-words, and with det in det är soligt, \"it is sunny\".","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"en-words and ett-words","body":"Every noun is an en-word or an ett-word, and the article says which: en lägenhet, ett hus. About three nouns in four are en-words. For most nouns there is no rule, so learn each one with its article; some endings decide it: nouns in -het and -ing are en-words (en lägenhet, en våning), and nouns in -um are ett-words (ett museum). A compound takes the gender of its last part: ett rum, so ett sovrum.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"\"The\" is an ending","body":"Swedish says \"the\" at the end of the noun. An en-word adds -en, or -n after a vowel: lägenheten, trappan. An ett-word adds -et, or -t after a vowel: huset, köket. A short vowel keeps its long consonant, and spelling doubles it: rum, rummet. After i or på the definite form is usual where English says \"the\": i köket, in the kitchen.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"The adjective agrees","body":"After en, or with an en-word in the indefinite, an adjective has no ending: en röd tröja. With an ett-word it adds -t: ett rött paraply. In the plural it adds -a: röda skor. A long vowel becomes short before -t: grön, grönt. After a vowel, d or t, spelling writes tt: blå, blått; röd, rött; vit, vitt. blå has the plural blå or blåa. After den or a possessive the -a form is used too: min röda tröja.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"Five plurals","body":"Plurals fall into groups. Most en-words in -a take -or: gurka, gurkor. Many other en-words take -ar (korv, korvar) or -er (banan, bananer). An ett-word ending in an unstressed vowel adds -n: äpple, äpplen; one stressed on its last vowel takes -er: paraply, paraplyer. An ett-word ending in a consonant often stays the same: ett ägg, två ägg. Learn each noun with its plural.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"My, your, our","body":"min, din, vår and er agree with the noun like an adjective: min bror, mitt hus, mina föräldrar. hans (his) and hennes (her) never change. The grandparents are named by side: mormor is the mother's mother and farmor the father's mother.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"Plurals that change the vowel","body":"A few nouns change their vowel in the plural: en hand, händer; en fot, fötter; en tand, tänder. öga and öra have the old plurals ögon and öron. These are learnt by heart. Like most words that were one syllable in Old Norse, händer, fötter and tänder take accent 1.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"Half past is half to","body":"Swedish counts the half hour towards the next hour: halv tre is half past two. Quarters are kvart över (past) and kvart i (to). For the parts of the day, på takes the definite form: på morgonen, på kvällen, på natten. In everyday speech the day names lose their g: måndag is said /ˈmɔ̌nda/.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"One form for every person","body":"A Swedish verb has one present form for every person: jag talar, du talar, vi talar. Verbs whose stem ends in a vowel take -r (talar, jobbar); most others take -er (läser, skriver), and a stem ending in r takes nothing (kör). With a job there is no article: jag är lärare.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"Telling someone to do something","body":"The order form is the verb without its -a: ringa, ring!; komma, kom!; springa, spring! A verb whose stem itself ends in -a keeps it: vänta!, stanna! In Sweden the emergency number is 112, and the h of hj is silent: hjälp /jɛlp/.","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}

{"title":"Where things are","body":"till vänster and till höger are to the left and to the right, and rakt fram is straight on. A building or a town ligger, lies, where it is: Var ligger banken? Prepositions of place: bredvid (next to), mellan (between), framför (in front of), bakom (behind).","sources":[{"title":"Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen","url":"https://lexin.nada.kth.se/lexin/"},{"title":"Wiktionary (Swedish entries)","url":"https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Wiktionary:Main_Page"}]}
